extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, journal editors, and academic publishing professionals interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A category/news-page compiling reports of retractions, withdrawals, and publication-misconduct incidents in mathematics, summarizing causes (plagiarism, fake peer review, errors) and governance disputes. Useful for tracking patterns of misconduct and editorial/publisher actions in math publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (including from older/unpublished theses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers retracted for closely resembling or copying prior work (example: 'plagiarizing a 50-year-old thesis' / closely resembled an unpublished 1968 dissertation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices cite close resemblance to pre-existing dissertations or publications as grounds for removal. Examples show institutions and journals issue retraction statements when substantial overlap with prior work is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faked peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of fabricated or fraudulent peer-review processes to get papers accepted (noted as 'faked peer review').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances of faked peer review have led to multiple retractions across journals; overlapping problems in sets of papers (plagiarism plus faked review) indicate systemic abuse of the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contaminated peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review processes compromised or 'contaminated' such that inappropriate evaluations or manipulated reviews influenced publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals have retracted papers when investigations find peer review was contaminated; contaminated review is cited alongside other issues (e.g., manipulated results) as cause for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake or manipulated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers containing fabricated data, manipulated figures, or otherwise falsified results (example phrasing: 'fake and manipulated results').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such findings undermine the validity of conclusions and have prompted journal retractions; investigations into numerical schemes or results can reveal manipulation that necessitates removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of the mathematics / substantive mathematical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that the core mathematics in a paper are incorrect or lack integrity (phrased as 'integrity of the mathematics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may retract articles when the mathematical arguments are shown to be flawed or unreliable. This includes discoveries of crucial mistakes, 'subtle inaccuracies', or proofs that do not hold up under scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial authenticity and authorship issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems with authorship such as ghost/phantom authors or authors who cannot be located (example: 'the author no one can find').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship irregularities—including false identities, unclear contributions, or overlapping problematic authorship across multiple papers—are grounds for investigation and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal due to discovered mistakes versus formal retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors or servers withdrawing work after discovering errors (e.g., 'withdrawn due to a crucial mistake' or authors requesting retractions for 'subtle inaccuracies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction between an author-initiated withdrawal and a publisher/journal retraction matters procedurally; withdrawals may be immediate on servers like arXiv, while formal retractions require publisher processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics gaming and broader fraudulent publishing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaming bibliometric measures and other fraudulent publishing behaviors (referred to as 'metrics gaming' and 'fraudulent publishing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working groups and articles recommend detection and mitigation strategies; such gaming is framed as undermining trust in science and as a target for community-level recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial governance and publisher interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about publisher decisions and governance that prompt editorial-board actions (example: editorial board resignations over Elsevier's 'concerning and potentially detrimental' decisions; replacement of EIC after term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial independence, hiring/appointment practices, and publisher oversight (e.g., 'designated publishers ... oversee a portfolio') are evaluated as part of healthy journal governance; perceived interference can lead to mass resignations and reputational issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness, clarity, and processing of retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether retraction notices are issued promptly and whether online versions are clearly marked (example: editors posted a notice but 'online versions of the papers still show no signs of having been retracted' while awaiting publisher processing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays or opaque handling of retractions (editors waiting on publishers to process notices) are criticized; clear, timely retraction statements and marking of affected articles are implied standards for good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of repeated misconduct (multiple retractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors with multiple retractions or repeated problematic publications (example: a 'third paper retracted' for a highly cited researcher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated retractions by the same author or in the same venue indicate systemic problems and affect credibility; patterns can inform stricter scrutiny and policy responses by journals and institutions.
